schools.summary: Gregory reads the good hearer as an 'even umpire' who keeps the ear of truth among the thorns; so Job treads down his own defence and sanctions Bildad's true sentiments — man put with God is not justified, for compared with the Author of all good he loses his righteousness.
Gill: without noticing Bildad's harsh censures Job enters directly into the argument, granting some things, confuting others, and defending his conduct.

Henry: Job agrees with Bildad's principle that God never perverts judgment — 'I know it is so of a truth'; we should own how far we agree with an adversary and not resist a truth for being urged against us.
Clarke lays out the chapter's movement — God's justice and man's sinfulness, the almighty power in earth and heaven, the affliction of innocent and wicked alike, and the complaint of his lot.

themes: the even umpire of the good hearer

schools.summary: Gill: Job knew 'of a truth,' most certainly, that God is just in all his ways, and kept it in sight amid his afflictions, needing no instruction in the article.
Keil and Delitzsch hear irony — 'yea, indeed, I know it is thus'; should God enter controversy, man could not answer one of a thousand, being confounded and disarmed by reason.
Clarke: compared with the immaculate holiness of God all Job's righteousness is nothing; Wesley: no man is absolutely just if God be severe to mark what is amiss.
Henry takes 'how should man be just with God?' as a pious confession of man's sinfulness rather than a passionate complaint of God's severity, though owning that peevish expressions do escape Job.

debates.question: Is 'how should man be just with God?' a murmur against God's severity or a confession of human sinfulness?

sides.position: a passionate complaint of God's strictness and severity
a pious confession of man's sinfulness — no flesh living justified

themes: I know it is so of a truth
how should man be just with God

schools.summary: Henry: God can ask a thousand puzzling questions (as from the whirlwind) and lay a thousand charges; man cannot set one aside but must plead guilty, laying his hand on his mouth.
Gill: whether God contend with man or man with God — a potsherd with its maker — the match is unequal, and there is no striving with God in a judicial way.
Clarke: of a thousand offences man cannot vindicate himself in one — hence the necessity of justification by faith; Wesley: one accusation among a thousand God shall produce.
Ellicott lets the phrase carry both senses — 'one question of a thousand, once in a thousand times.'

themes: cannot answer one of a thousand

schools.summary: Gill: God essentially and perfectly wise, infinite in understanding, disappointing all devices and seeing every thought — how can sinful men be just before him on their own righteousness?
Henry: 'who hath hardened himself against him and hath prospered?' — no daring sinner ever did; apostate angels, the dragon cast out, briers set before a consuming fire.
Clarke: by infinite knowledge God sees all, by almighty power punishes all; he that rebels against him must be destroyed.

themes: wise in heart and mighty in strength
none hardened against God and prospered

schools.summary: Gill offers literal instances — a Helvetian village buried in 1618, the Mount of Olives removed (Zech. 14:4), the Flood — or a proverb of God's power.

Henry: the mountains the emblem of fixedness, yet removed 'and they know not' — Sinai shook, the hills skipped, the everlasting mountains scattered; enough to say Job speaks of what God can do, though the Flood best answers if we read fact.

Clarke refers it to earthquakes, mountains and islands removed in an instant, 'they know not' the suddenness; Wesley: removed suddenly, 'in anger' the token of displeasure with the men who dwell on them.

debates.question: Are the removed mountains literal upheavals or an image of divine power?

sides.position: literal convulsions — earthquake, the Flood, the rending of Olivet
a proverb of what God can do, held with the literal as possible

schools.summary: Gill: God will shake the earth from her place at the last day (Rev. 20:11), not by common partial earthquakes, and the verse may glance at the Flood (2 Pet. 3:7).
Keil and Delitzsch gather the strophe into one sweep of solitary omnipotence — shaking the earth, commanding the sun, sealing the stars, spreading the heavens, and treading the sea.

Clarke: the trembling pillars refer to an earthquake and its warning tremor, most likely literal; Wesley: 'the earth' great portions of it, and 'the pillars' the deep inward parts that support the surface.

outliers.note: Notes the Scriptural idiom by which earthquakes may signify commotions in states, mountains rulers, the sun empires, and the stars petty states — but judges the expressions here most likely literal.

themes: shaking the earth out of her place

schools.summary: Gill: God could suspend the sun (Joshua's long day, Hezekiah's shadow), or it rises only at his command; or eclipses, the Egyptian darkness, and the Flood's forty days are meant.
Clarke: 'commandeth the sun' = obscures it with clouds, darkness, or an eclipse; 'sealeth up the stars' = wrapped and sealed like a letter that cannot be read.
Ellicott: 'sealeth up the stars' (cf. Job 41:15) carries the idea of shutting up, of taking away their power.
Gill reads 'spreadeth out the heavens' of continuance — God keeps them spread like a curtain and tent (Ps. 104:2), and 'alone,' without any creature's help.

Keil and Delitzsch reject Ewald and Hirzel's 'walking above the thunder-clouds' (Ps. 18:10), reading the first clause of the creation of the firmament so the verb means to expand; Ellicott renders 'high place of the sea,' the sea when it runs mountains high.

Clarke finds a majestic image, God stepping from billow to billow, though David outdoes Job (Ps. 29:10; 18:9-15); Wesley reads a black tempestuous season, 'treadeth' being to repress and rule the raging waters.

debates.question: Does God 'tread the high places of the sea' or walk the cloud-heights above the thunder?

sides.position: the storm-tossed sea trodden underfoot
the heights of the cloud-sea, above the thunder-clouds
holders: Ewald (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Hirzel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

outliers.note: Judges David greater than Job even here — 'Job is great, but in every respect David is greater' — setting Psalm 29:10 and Psalm 18:9-15 above Job's image of treading the sea.

themes: treading the waves of the sea

schools.summary: Gill: 'Arcturus' a constellation (Bar Tzemach, Ben Melech; 'Arcturus and his sons,' Job 38:32) in the Bear's tail; Aben Ezra took it for the seven stars.

Clarke spreads the versions and inclines to Parkhurst and Bate — kimah warmth, ash parching air, kesil rigid cold, the chambers thick clouds — not constellations at all, and reports Hales's Taurus/Scorpio dating; Wesley names them constellations of greatest eminency comprehending all the stars.
Ellicott finds real astronomical knowledge — the Bear (north), Orion (south), the Pleiades (east), the chambers unknown regions; Keil and Delitzsch render 'the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades.'

debates.question: Do Ash, Kesil, and Kimah name the constellations, or something else?

sides.position: the great constellations — the Bear/Arcturus, Orion, the Pleiades
qualities of weather — genial heat, parching air, rigid cold, and clouds
holders: Parkhurst and Bate (as reported by Clarke)

sides.position: Taurus and Scorpio, fixing Job's date to 2337 B.C.

outliers.note: Prefers Parkhurst and Bate's view that Ash, Kesil, and Kimah are not constellations at all but denote heat, parching air, cold, and the thick clouds of the south, and warns that Hales's astronomical dating rests on the unproved assumption that they are stars.

schools.summary: Ellicott: Job adopts the very words his former antagonist Eliphaz had used at Job 5:9.
Wesley: Job says the same as Eliphaz, in the very same Hebrew words, to show his full agreement touching the divine perfections.
Gill: 'great things past finding out' in creation, providence, and grace, past number and past expression.
Henry: God does many things and great, to admiration, and Job does not decline to speak after his adversary — 'O the depth of his counsels!'
Gill: the invisibility of God — his essence unseen and incomprehensible, though seen by faith in Christ the image of the invisible God.
Ellicott: 'he passeth on' is again Eliphaz's phrase (Job 4:15); the Book of Job lays the foundation of the Gospel by overthrowing man's standing-ground in himself.

Clarke: God is incomprehensible in all his ways and works, and must be so if he be God; Wesley: 'goeth' by providence in mercy or judgment, 'passeth' from one action to another, spoken after the manner of men.

themes: he goeth by me and I see him not

schools.summary: Gill: what God never takes (his love, grace, Christ, the spiritual blessings) versus the temporal blessings he takes at pleasure — children, wealth, health, and life itself.
Henry: incontestable sovereignty — 'the Lord takes away, and who can hinder him?'; God is not obliged to give a reason (Dan. 4:35).
Clarke: God never gives but ever lends, recalling the misused gift; supreme, wise, kind, and good, questioned by none; Wesley: who can restrain or reprove him? far be it to quarrel with God.

Keil and Delitzsch: God works among men as in nature, supremely, invisibly, irresistibly (Isa. 45:9); Ellicott: even were God in the wrong he would maintain his cause by might and crush his adversary.

themes: he taketh away, who can hinder him

schools.summary: Gill: God withdraws his anger from his own people but never from the wicked, who are punished with everlasting destruction.
Henry: God the Lord of his anger; the proud helpers, kings and rulers leagued against him (Ps. 2), stoop and fall with those they meant to help.

Ellicott: 'proud helpers' is literally 'helpers of Rahab' (Isa. 30:7; Ps. 87:4) — whether Egypt or a name for the lost archangel is impossible to say; the phrase expresses the ideal of strength, the giants.
Clarke: no use to contend with God, all his opposers must perish; Wesley: 'helpers' those who uphold one another against him, who fall and are crushed.

debates.question: Who are the 'helpers of Rahab' that stoop under God?

sides.position: Egypt, with a probable allusion to Pharaoh's overthrow
a poetical name for the lost archangel, or the giant-strength of the proud

themes: God will not withdraw his anger

schools.summary: Gill: if the great and even the infernal powers must stoop, how should a poor feeble creature enter the lists and answer any charge exhibited against him?
Henry: Job durst not dispute — shall the clay or the broken vessel reason with the potter? Let all flesh be silent before him.
Clarke: 'I cannot contend with my Maker; he is Lawgiver and Judge'; Wesley: since none can resist his power or comprehend his ways, how can I answer his arguments?

themes: how much less shall I answer him

schools.summary: Gill: not the righteousness of his cause nor of his Redeemer, but his own legal and civil righteousness Job will not urge, since on that ground no man living is justified.

Clarke: though clear of the crimes charged, he would not dare stand before God's immaculate holiness, but cry 'cleanse thou me from secret faults'; Wesley: God knows him better than he knows himself, so he would only make supplication.
Ellicott: putting the case that Job were actually righteous, yet even then supplication, and not assertion, would best become him.
Henry: Job knew too much of God to stand a trial and too much of himself to insist on his justification; the innocent man's wisest posture is to beseech his Judge, not answer him.

themes: though righteous, I would not answer
no man justified on his own righteousness

schools.summary: Gill: Broughton reads a doubting question, 'if I cry, will he answer me?'; yet Job was a praying man who had found God a hearer of prayer, and only questions whether he would be heard in this extremity.

Clarke: 'I could scarcely suppose he could condescend to notice a being so mean' — a sense confuting the friends' charge of presumption; Wesley: Job could not believe his desire granted while still full of the tokens of God's displeasure, and would think it a dream.

Henry: God answers before we call and not because we call; even had the thing been granted, Job would not believe his own voice had done it, but that it was for God's name's sake (so also Bishop Patrick).

themes: if I had called and he had answered
not for our prayers but for his name
the majesty that dwarfs the suppliant

schools.summary: Gill hears in the tempest Job's own calamity — perhaps the wind that felled the house — and Schultens's 'burning tempest' that blackens the flesh like a coal.

Ellicott notes 'breaketh' a rare verb found in only three passages (Gen. 3:15; Ps. 139:11); Keil and Delitzsch render the strophe of God crushing him in a tempest and multiplying wounds without cause.

Clarke lays the stress on 'without cause' — it is cruel to say Job suffers for his crimes when the text denies any known reason; Wesley: without any special cause of such singular affliction, not the extraordinary guilt his friends charged.
Henry warns that here Job spoke unadvisedly, charging God with wounding him 'without cause' — a passion the following verses only heighten.
Gill: whether Job's asthma or the hot burning winds that almost take away a man's breath, the design is to show his afflictions continued and without interval.
Clarke: 'I have no respite; I suffer continually in body and my mind is incessantly harassed'; Wesley: my pains are continual, without so much as a breathing time free from them.
Ellicott takes the action as the recovering of breath after complete exhaustion, and carries it into the argument that for man to maintain his righteousness before God is to proclaim his iniquity.
Henry hears the excess of passion as well as the truth — a good man charging God with a cruelty of continuance, whom God will afterward give leave to unsay by repentance.

themes: not suffered to take his breath

schools.summary: Gill: no disputing with God on the foot of strength, for even the weakness of God is stronger than men, and Job is feeble in body, mind, and estate.

Clarke glosses 'who shall set me a time' as 'who would be a witness for me?' and notes the forensic terms of the whole passage; Wesley: no superior judge can summon God and man together and set a time to plead.
Ellicott owns the passage abrupt and enigmatical — God is judge and court together — and sees in Job's confidence-in-innocence-yet-certainty-of-condemnation the very attitude the Gospel vindicates.

themes: the forensic language of the courts

schools.summary: Gill: if Job seek justification by his own righteousness and pronounce himself righteous, what would it signify? The plea recoils upon the pleader.
Clarke reads a submission — 'God must have some reason; I do not pretend to justify myself; the attempt would insult his majesty'; Wesley takes 'justify' of pleading his own innocency against God.
Ellicott sharpens the paradox: to say 'I am perfect' would prove Job perverse by the very saying, the finite unable to come into competition with the Infinite.

Henry: the godly man will not justify himself before God, for all are concluded under sin; yet the accent of complaint here begins to make it a question of might, not right — the first evil fruit of a self-righteous spirit Job is later reproved for.

outliers.note: Marks that Job's answer, sound as far as it confesses man's inability to be justified, begins to imply that the question between the sufferer and the Lord of providence is one of might and not of right — the first appearance of the self-righteous spirit for which he is afterward reproved.

themes: mine own mouth shall condemn me

schools.summary: Gill takes it as a case merely supposed — though Job were really and truly perfect, conscious of no sin, yet he would not stand upon it before God.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the usual reading, a bold assertion of innocence in scorn of life (Schnurrer, Hirzel, Ewald, Schlottmann), against their own — 'I know not my soul,' Job become a mystery to himself; and 'this is one thing' means 'it is all one whether man is innocent or not.'

Clarke: had Job the fullest conviction of blamelessness, he would not plead it nor think it security for a prolonged life; Wesley: he would not acknowledge his own soul, but only make supplication, abhorring his life rather than trust his own integrity.

debates.question: Does 'I would not know my soul' assert innocence in scorn of life, or confess a self grown a riddle?

sides.position: a bold assertion of innocence, careless of a life grown hateful
holders: Schnurrer (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Hirzel (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Ewald (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)
Schlottmann (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: 'I know not my soul, myself' — his innocence become a mystery he cannot read

themes: though perfect, I would not know my soul
it is all one, innocent or not

schools.summary: Gill: the 'one thing' is one event alike to righteous and wicked — whether perfect or not, a man is equally liable to be afflicted; on God's justice Job agreed with his friends.

Henry states the dispute exactly and grants its truth — temporal judgments fall on good and bad alike, Josiah as well as Ahab — but faults the manner: 'he destroys' overstates 'he afflicts,' for God does not afflict willingly.

Clarke: observation shows the righteous and wicked have an equal lot when sudden calamity comes, with few exceptions; Wesley: in this one thing Job must contend — God sends afflictions promiscuously on good and bad men.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'the innocent and the wicked he destroyeth,' and read Job's own swiftly passing life as the instance.

outliers.note: Grants the maxim largely true but faults its passion: when Job meant that God afflicts, he ought not to have said 'he destroys' the perfect and the wicked, for God does not afflict willingly; when the spirit is heated, we need a watch before our lips.

themes: he destroyeth the perfect and the wicked
all things come alike to all
the point in dispute with the friends
truth spoken with too much passion

schools.summary: Gill reads the 'scourge' of any sore calamity that slays suddenly, and leaves the harder clause unpressed, noting some restrain the slaying to the wicked.
Henry takes the laughing favourably — God well pleased to see the same scourge that is the wicked's perdition be the innocent's trial of faith, unto praise and honour (cf. Job 5:22).

Ellicott reads it as Job's dark rhetoric of a God who 'laughs at it,' taking no more notice than if it were sport — the argument of a man who for the debate takes the pessimist view, yet holds fast his faith and is justified at the last (Job 42:8).
Wesley: God is well pleased to see the same scourge that is the wicked's perdition prove the innocent's trial of faith, found unto praise and honour and glory.

debates.question: What does it mean that God 'laughs at the trial of the innocent'?

sides.position: God is pleased, as a refiner, at the faith his stroke proves in the innocent
an appearance of divine indifference, flung out in Job's overstrained rhetoric

themes: laughing at the trial of the innocent

schools.summary: Gill: 'the wicked' may be Satan the god of this world (Jarchi, Bar Tzemach), a tyrant such as Nimrod, or wicked men in general; the giving or taking of the earth is no proof of a man's goodness or wickedness.

Clarke: the worst men possess most of this world's goods, so prosperity is no mark of God's favour; the covering of the judges' faces is a judicial blinding God permits, not works; Wesley: the wicked advanced while the wise and good are buried in obscurity.

Henry holds the paradox — the wicked have the earth, the righteous have heaven — and, with Bishop Patrick and the Assembly's Annotations, thinks the 'wicked one' may be some noted tyrant of Job's day.

debates.question: Who is 'the wicked' into whose hand the earth is given?

sides.position: Satan, the god of this world
a particular tyrant known to Job (Nimrod, or a prosperous oppressor of his day)
holders: the Assembly's Annotations (as reported by Henry)

sides.position: wicked men in general, who hold most of the earth

themes: the earth given to the wicked
covering the faces of the judges
Satan, a tyrant, or the wicked at large

schools.summary: Gill: the 'post' a runner or courier swift of foot or horse, yet Job's days — especially his prosperous days (Broughton) — are swifter still, gone as soon as come.
Henry allows the complaint proper — all Job's good days gone, no trace remaining, like an eagle in the air or a ship in the sea (Prov. 30:19); how swift time's motion, how vain its enjoyments.
Clarke: 'a runner,' the courier; the Chaldee's shadow of a flying bird; irreparable time flies away (Virgil); Wesley: 'they see no good,' seeing put for experiencing good or evil.
Ellicott marks the pivot — with 'swifter than a post' Job turns away from the contemplation of God and his dealings to that of his own misery.

themes: the turn to his own misery

schools.summary: Gill: light swift vessels — Bar Tzemach's oar-driven 'ships of desire,' or ships so swift they reach the haven at a wish, or 'ships of enmity,' pirate craft unladen and therefore fast.
Ellicott owns 'ships of Eveh' a mystery, perhaps a Nile boat (Job's acquaintance with Egypt); Keil and Delitzsch render 'ships of reeds,' the papyrus skiffs.

Clarke sets the 'inflated ships' leaving no track against a variant in 47 manuscripts and the Syriac, 'hostile ships' that strip and flee, favoured by the eagle image; Wesley reads the eagle as the swiftest bird in sight of its prey.

debates.question: What are the 'swift ships' Job's days are compared to?

sides.position: the light reed-boats of the Nile, leaving no trace behind
pirate or hostile ships that strip and flee under full sail

themes: the eagle hasting to the prey

schools.summary: Gill: Job attempts to forget the causes of his complaint — his losses — to cease complaining, bury them in oblivion, and change his note to a gladder key.
Clarke: 'I will forego my complaining, leave off my heaviness,' and with the Vulgate 'change my countenance,' forcing himself to smile and assume the appearance of comfort.

Henry: Job did his endeavour to quiet and compose himself, as his friends advised, that he might be fit for converse with God and man; but fear and sorrow are tyrannising things, not easily brought into subjection.

themes: the honest attempt to be comforted

schools.summary: Gill: Job feared his sorrows would return, surround, and overwhelm him, that they would increase and abide and he should never be released.

Clarke hears a further fear — lest none of his works, however well intended, stand God's scrutiny; and 'thou wilt not hold me innocent' means God will not acquit him so as to take away his affliction; Wesley: God will not clear his innocency by removing the afflictions — words of despair and impatience.
Henry: the brave resolve breaks — 'when I strive most against my trouble, it prevails most over me and proves too hard for me.'

themes: thou wilt not hold me innocent

schools.summary: Gill: if Job be the hypocrite they think, vain to supplicate, for God hears not sinners; or, more likely, if God will not hold him innocent, vain to labour to prove his integrity, the verdict being fixed.

Clarke: 'if I am the sinner you suppose, in vain should I labour to counterfeit joy and cease to complain'; Wesley: 'I shall be used like a wicked man still; why comfort myself with vain hopes of deliverance?'
Henry: it is to no purpose to speak in a cause already prejudged — yet not so with God, the patron of oppressed innocency, to whom a righteous cause is never committed in vain.

themes: if I be wicked, why labour in vain
prayer, feigned joy, or self-defence all vain
the righteous cause not vain with God

schools.summary: Gill: let Job wash with snow water or by any method, his iniquity is still marked before God; no ablution, duty, or even repentance can purify the heart before a holy God.

Clarke: snow water reckoned more detergent, and (with Good) an allusion to washing the hands in innocence (Ps. 26:6; Pilate, Matt. 27:24); Wesley: though Job clear himself before men, it avails nothing before God.

Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence into the strophe — though he wash with snow water and lye, God would plunge him into the pit, for God is not a man to be answered, nor is there an arbitrator between them.
Henry: God who knows the heart can charge us with secret sin enough to strip all pretension to purity — as the commandment did to Paul the Pharisee, plunging him in the ditch.

themes: secret sin before the holy God

schools.summary: Gill: set against God's perfect purity Job would appear exceedingly impure, held out as the filth of the world by continued affliction; or the 'ditch' is affliction itself, his ulcers or deeper troubles.

Clarke: tried by the eye of God Job would be found as a leper, his own clothes dreading to touch him — a bold figure from his diseased body; Wesley: so filthy that his clothes, had they sense, would abhor to touch him.
Henry: Job's own bitter reading of his afflictions, the things that blackened him before his friends; yet God, who knows the heart, can charge secret sin enough to plunge the cleanest in the ditch.

themes: mine own clothes shall abhor me

schools.summary: Gill: God is a Spirit, infinite, immortal, pure and holy, whereas Job is finite, feeble, mortal, and sinful; the potsherds may strive with their equals but not with their Creator, who sees impurity where man sees none.

Henry: God is not a man as we are; of the greatest princes we may say 'they are men as we,' but not of God, whose thoughts and ways are infinitely above ours — a consideration that should keep us humble and silent before him.
Wesley: God is one infinitely superior in majesty, power, wisdom, and justice, so that Job should not presume to debate his cause or come face to face to plead on equal terms.

themes: he is not a man, as I am

schools.summary: Gill: a 'daysman' must be wiser and mightier than the two he judges between, and there is none among angels or men wiser and mightier than God, so no umpire can stand between Job and his Maker.

Clarke fixes the legal term and notes fifteen manuscripts with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic reading the wish, 'O that there were!' — poor Job not yet knowing the one Mediator (1 Tim. 2:5); Wesley: the Lord Jesus is now that blessed daysman who has laid his hand on both.

Henry hears the complaint that there is none as a wish that there were, reads the Septuagint's 'O that there were a mediator,' and points to Christ, the daysman to whom the Father has committed all judgment.

debates.question: Does the text state there is no daysman, or wish for one?

sides.position: 'there is not any daysman betwixt us' (the received text)
'O that there were a daysman!' (fifteen manuscripts with the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic)

themes: the umpire wiser and mightier than both

schools.summary: Gill: not the government of God, of which the rod is the ensign, but the rod of affliction Job asks removed, which so depressed his spirit that he could not reason freely.

Clarke notes the large letter in 'his rod' (the Masora's nine calamities) and the sceptre of majesty on the judgment-seat, so appalling that Job cannot speak (Isa. 6:1); Wesley: 'let him not deal with me by his perfect justice, but by his grace and clemency.'

Henry: the 'rod' is less Job's outward affliction than the load on his spirit from the apprehension of God's wrath; let him recover the sight of mercy, and then he could order his cause — but it is not so with him.

themes: let him take his rod away
the rod of affliction or of wrath

schools.summary: Gill: were the terror lifted Job could speak without servile fear, so as to defend himself; he hears too the believer's liberty at the throne of grace when the terror of justice is removed.
Keil and Delitzsch render the close simply, 'then would I speak, and not fear him; but it is not so with me' — the resolve to speak at once withdrawn.

Clarke: 'I am not in such circumstances as to plead with my Judge,' prizing Coverdale's 'as long as I am in such fearfulness, I can make no answer' — a picture of the penitent soul, terror-seized before God's majesty.

outliers.note: Owns the closing phrase 'it is not so with me' variously understood — 'I am not thus without fear,' or 'I am not so as ye suppose, but innocent,' or 'am I not right with myself?' — the self-consciousness he voices again at Job 10:1.

themes: then would I speak and not fear
but it is not so with me
